quests.sentence: She parks her car in the garage.
quests.hint: Add the object right after the verb, then say where the action happens.
quests.explanation: Her car (object) follows parks directly, and in the garage (place) comes last — the standard order is verb, object, then place.

quests.sentence: He submits the report at the front desk.
quests.hint: The thing being submitted comes before the location where it's submitted.
quests.explanation: The report (object) comes right after submits, and at the front desk (place) follows it, keeping object before place.

quests.sentence: The waiter serves the dessert at their table.
quests.hint: Keep the same order: verb, then what is served, then where it's served.
quests.explanation: The dessert (object) precedes at the table (place), matching the object-then-place pattern from the previous two sentences.

quests.sentence: She submits her assignment by Friday.
quests.hint: Say what is being submitted first, then attach the deadline information at the end.
quests.explanation: Her homework (object) comes right after submits, and by Friday (time) closes the sentence, following object-then-time order.

quests.sentence: He renews his passport every five years.
quests.hint: The object still comes before the time expression, even when the time phrase has three words.
quests.explanation: His passport (object) precedes every five years (time), showing that a longer time expression doesn't change its end position after the object.

quests.sentence: The company releases its earnings report every quarter.
quests.hint: A longer object phrase still comes before the time expression that closes the sentence.
quests.explanation: Its earnings report (a three-word object) still comes before every quarter (time), confirming the object always precedes the time phrase.

quests.sentence: She works from home on Fridays.
quests.hint: With no object, place comes right after the verb, and time follows the place.
quests.explanation: From home (place) follows works directly, and on Fridays (time) comes last — without an object, place moves right next to the verb.

quests.sentence: They travel abroad every summer.
quests.hint: Abroad acts as a place word by itself, with no preposition needed, and time still comes after it.
quests.explanation: Abroad functions as a place expression without a preposition, and every summer (time) follows it, keeping the place-before-time order.

quests.sentence: He commutes to the city every weekday.
quests.hint: To the city names the destination first, then every weekday tells us when it happens.
quests.explanation: To the city (place) comes directly after commutes, and every weekday (time) follows, again placing place before time.

quests.sentence: Every Monday the team reviews the budget.
quests.hint: A time expression can open the sentence instead of ending it — put it first, then the usual subject-verb-object.
quests.explanation: Every Monday (time) leads the sentence here, followed by the normal the team reviews the budget — fronting the time phrase for emphasis.

quests.sentence: Each spring the school hosts a science fair.
quests.hint: The same fronting pattern works with any time phrase: time phrase first, then subject, verb, object.
quests.explanation: Each spring (time) opens the sentence, and the school hosts a science fair follows in its usual subject-verb-object order.

quests.sentence: Twice a year the clinic offers free checkups.
quests.hint: Even a three-word time phrase like twice a year can front the sentence the same way.
quests.explanation: Twice a year (a longer time expression) still fronts the sentence, followed by the clinic offers free checkups in normal order.

quests.sentence: She meets her clients at the coffee shop every Thursday.
quests.hint: Stack all four parts in order: verb, object, then place, then time, one after another.
quests.explanation: Her clients (object), at the coffee shop (place), and every Thursday (time) follow meets in that exact sequence — the full object-place-time chain.
quests.grammarRule: Full Chain: Subject + Verb + Object + Place + Time

quests.sentence: He delivers the packages to the warehouse every morning.
quests.hint: The same four-part chain repeats with new vocabulary: object, then place, then time.
quests.explanation: The packages (object), to the warehouse (place), and every morning (time) follow delivers in the same fixed sequence as the previous sentence.
quests.grammarRule: Full Chain: Subject + Verb + Object + Place + Time

quests.sentence: The teacher grades the assignments in the staff room every evening.
quests.hint: A longer, two-word place phrase doesn't disturb the object-place-time sequence.
quests.explanation: The assignments (object), in the staff room (a two-word place), and every evening (time) still follow grades in the established order.
quests.grammarRule: Full Chain: Subject + Verb + Object + Place + Time

quests.sentence: She works in an office on the third floor.
quests.hint: When two place details appear together, the bigger location comes first and the specific detail comes second.
quests.explanation: In an office (general place) comes before on the third floor (specific detail), moving from the broader location to the more precise one.

quests.sentence: He teaches at a school near the stadium.
quests.hint: The broader place phrase leads, and the more specific detail about it follows.
quests.explanation: At a school (general place) precedes near the stadium (a more specific detail about its location), following the general-to-specific order.

quests.sentence: They live in an apartment above the bakery.
quests.hint: Start with the general place, then narrow down with a more specific detail about it.
quests.explanation: In an apartment (general place) comes first, and above the bakery (specific detail) narrows it down, keeping the general-to-specific pattern.

quests.sentence: She calls her parents at eight every evening.
quests.hint: When two time details appear together, the exact time comes first and the frequency comes second.
quests.explanation: At eight (a specific time) comes before every evening (a frequency expression), moving from the precise clock time to how often it repeats.

quests.sentence: The bus departs at noon every weekday.
quests.hint: The exact time leads, and the how-often expression follows right after it.
quests.explanation: At noon (specific time) precedes every weekday (frequency), following the same specific-then-frequency order.

quests.sentence: He takes his medication at breakfast every day.
quests.hint: A named part of the day still counts as the specific time and comes before the frequency word.
quests.explanation: At breakfast (a specific point in the daily routine) comes before every day (frequency), keeping the exact-time-then-frequency pattern.

quests.sentence: The train travels from London to Paris.
quests.hint: From marks the starting point and to marks the destination — from always comes first.
quests.explanation: From London names the starting point and to Paris names the destination; from consistently precedes to in this range structure.

quests.sentence: She works from nine to five.
quests.hint: The same from-to pattern works for time ranges, not just places.
quests.explanation: From nine to five expresses a time range using the identical from-then-to structure used for places like from London to Paris.

quests.sentence: The store operates from Monday to Saturday.
quests.hint: Days of the week can form a range too, using the same from-to order.
quests.explanation: From Monday to Saturday shows a range of days, following the same from-before-to pattern already seen with places and clock times.

quests.sentence: The airline flies passengers from Chicago to Tokyo twice a week.
quests.hint: Combine object, then the from-to range, then a frequency expression, all trailing the verb.
quests.explanation: Passengers (object) comes first, from Chicago to Tokyo (the range) follows, and twice a week (frequency) closes the sentence — three elements in sequence.

quests.sentence: The courier delivers packages from the warehouse to local stores every afternoon.
quests.hint: The object leads, then the from-to range names both ends of the delivery route, then time closes it.
quests.explanation: Packages (object), from the warehouse to local stores (the full range), and every afternoon (time) follow delivers in that exact order.

quests.sentence: The shuttle takes employees from the parking lot to headquarters every hour.
quests.hint: The parking lot is a two-word location, but the other end of a from-to range can be just one word — the pattern still holds.
quests.explanation: Employees (object) comes first, from the parking lot to headquarters (a range ending in a single-word destination) follows, and every hour (time) ends the sentence.

quests.sentence: Every weekday the manager reviews sales reports from each regional store.
quests.hint: Front the time expression, then follow with subject, verb, object, and a place phrase — reviewing two skills from this file.
quests.explanation: Every weekday (fronted time) opens the sentence, and the manager reviews sales reports from each regional store follows in ordinary subject-verb-object-place order.

quests.sentence: She commutes from her apartment to the office every weekday morning.
quests.hint: Combine the from-to range with a closing time expression, in the same order practiced earlier in this file.
quests.explanation: From her apartment to the office (the range) follows commutes, and every weekday morning (time) closes the sentence, reviewing the range-then-time pattern.

quests.sentence: The company ships orders from its warehouse to customers every business day.
quests.hint: Stack object, then the from-to range, then a frequency phrase — the same three-part chain from earlier, one more time.
quests.explanation: Orders (object), from its warehouse to customers (the range), and every business day (time) follow ships in the object-range-time sequence practiced throughout this file.
